title: §01-002: Java Syntax & OOP Fundamentals
description: Method overriding vs overloading, records, access modifiers, sealed classes, pattern matching, and value equality.

cards.question: What is the critical defect in declaring `public boolean equals(Point other)` instead of `public boolean equals(Object other)`?

options.text: The code fails to compile because `@Override` is required for all public methods.
It overloads `equals` instead of overriding `Object.equals(Object)`, causing collections like `HashSet` and `HashMap` to fall back to reference identity (`==`).
The JVM throws a `ClassCastException` whenever an element is placed into a collection.
The method is ignored by the JVM and garbage collected.

cards.explanation: Method overriding requires the exact parameter signature of the superclass method: `public boolean equals(Object o)`. Declaring `equals(Point other)` creates an overload. Because standard collections operate on `Object` references, they invoke `equals(Object)`, resulting in default reference identity comparison.
cards.pitfall: Always annotate `equals` with `@Override`. If you accidentally overload the method signature, the compiler will catch it immediately.
cards.citation: Effective Java (Bloch) Item 10 / Learning Java (Loy et al.) Ch. 5

cards.question: Why should `Double.compare(d1, d2) == 0` be used instead of `d1 == d2` when implementing `equals` for a class containing `double` fields?

options.text: Primitive `double` cannot be compared using `==` in Java.
`d1 == d2` evaluates `Double.NaN == Double.NaN` as `false`, violating reflexive equality in collections, whereas `Double.compare` treats `NaN` values as equal.
`Double.compare` converts double to `BigDecimal` automatically to avoid rounding drift.
`==` triggers memory boxing allocations on every check.

cards.explanation: Under IEEE 754 rules, `Double.NaN == Double.NaN` evaluates to `false`. However, the general contract of `equals` requires reflexivity (`x.equals(x)` must always be `true`). `Double.compare(Double.NaN, Double.NaN) == 0` correctly evaluates to `true`, maintaining collection integrity.
cards.pitfall: Never use primitive `==` on `float` or `double` fields inside `equals()`. Always use `Float.compare(f1, f2) == 0` and `Double.compare(d1, d2) == 0`.
cards.citation: Effective Java (Bloch) Item 10 & Item 11 / Java Language Specification §15.21.1

cards.question: In a Java `record`, what is the primary purpose of a compact constructor (e.g. `public Range { ... }` without a parameter list)?

options.text: To define private helper fields that are excluded from the canonical state vector.
To validate and normalize record components before the compiler automatically assigns them to fields.
To bypass final field initialization and enable mutable setters.
To allow the record to extend a custom abstract base class.

cards.explanation: A compact constructor omits the explicit parameter list and the boilerplate field assignments (`this.x = x`). Developers use it to validate invariants (e.g. checking for null or range boundaries) or normalize values. The compiler implicitly inserts field assignments at the end of the constructor block.
cards.pitfall: Do not attempt to write `this.low = low;` inside a compact constructor; assigning directly to record fields in a compact constructor results in a compilation error.
cards.citation: Java SE 21 Specification: Records (JEP 395) / Learning Java Ch. 5

cards.question: If a class member (field or method) has NO access modifier specified (default), what is its accessibility scope?

options.text: Visible to all classes in all packages across the entire module.
Visible only within the declaring class and all its subclasses regardless of package.
Visible to any class within the same package, but inaccessible to outside packages and subclasses in other packages.
Strictly private to the declaring class.

cards.explanation: The default access modifier in Java is package-private (no keyword). It allows access only from types located within the exact same package. Unlike `protected`, it does not grant access to subclasses located in different packages.
cards.pitfall: Developers coming from C++ or TypeScript often mistake package-private for `protected`. `protected` includes package access PLUS subclasses anywhere; default includes package access ONLY.
cards.citation: Effective Java (Bloch) Item 15: Minimize the accessibility of classes and members

cards.question: When defining a sealed interface `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square`, what modifier MUST every permitted subtype declare?

options.text: Every subtype must declare the `abstract` modifier.
Every subtype must declare exactly one of: `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
Every subtype must declare the `record` modifier.
Every subtype must declare `transient`.

cards.explanation: Java requires that every class or interface that extends/implements a sealed type explicitly specify its subclassing policy using one of three modifiers: `final` (prevents further subclassing), `sealed` (restricts subclassing to another specific set), or `non-sealed` (opens subclassing to any class).
cards.pitfall: Permitted classes must reside in the same package (or same named module) as the sealed supertype, otherwise compilation fails.

cards.concept: Pattern Matching for switch Null Handling
cards.question: In Java 21 pattern matching for `switch`, what happens by default if a `null` value is evaluated without an explicit `case null` branch?

options.text: It matches the `default` branch silently.
The switch expression throws a `NullPointerException` immediately.
The switch yields `null` without executing any branch.
It results in a compile-time syntax error.

cards.explanation: Historically and in modern pattern matching, a switch statement or expression throws `NullPointerException` if the selector expression evaluates to `null`, unless an explicit `case null` (or combined `case null, default`) branch is present.
cards.pitfall: Assuming `default` catches `null` in a switch. In Java, `default` only matches non-null values that do not match other patterns unless written as `case null, default:`.
cards.citation: Java SE 21 Specification: Pattern Matching for switch (JEP 441)

cards.question: What is a covariant return type in Java method overriding?

options.text: An overridden method can return a subtype of the return type declared in the superclass method.
An overridden method can accept broader parameter types than the superclass method.
A method can return multiple values simultaneously using tuples.
A method whose return type changes based on generic type arguments at runtime.

cards.explanation: Since Java 5, an overriding method is permitted to declare a return type that is a subtype of the superclass method's return type (covariance). This eliminates the need for callers to cast the returned object when invoking the method on the subclass type.
cards.pitfall: Covariance applies ONLY to return types, NEVER to parameter types. Altering parameter types creates an overload rather than an override.

cards.question: Where are `static` fields allocated in Java 8+, and how does their lifecycle differ from instance fields?

options.text: Static fields are allocated on the thread execution stack and destroyed when the method exits.
Static fields are stored with the Class object in the heap and persist as long as the loading ClassLoader remains alive.
Static fields are recreated every time `new` is called on the class.
Static fields are stored in the CPU registers.

cards.explanation: Static fields belong to the `Class` object rather than any individual instance. In Java 8+, `Class` objects and their static fields reside in the managed heap (with metadata in Metaspace) and remain accessible throughout the lifetime of the class's defining `ClassLoader`.
cards.pitfall: Storing large collections or caches in `static` fields without eviction is the leading cause of classloader memory leaks, as these objects cannot be collected until the class itself is unloaded.
cards.citation: Effective Java (Bloch) Item 7: Eliminate obsolete object references
